paras: The attempted lynching at Searcy was an effort by a party of men in Searcy, Arkansas, in December 1881 to hang an unnamed Black man at the urging of a visitor who offered to show the town's young men how to "hang a nigger." Before the hanging could be carried out, the lynchers were attacked by a large number of persons, and the instigator fled. The only known account is a mocking item in the Searcy Record, reprinted in the Memphis Daily Appeal.

According to the Searcy Record, a man who thought "the boys" of the town "a trifle slow" came in "a day or two ago" and proposed to show them how to "hang a nigger." A party was raised and "the victim was ready for the sacrifice," but the item gives neither his name nor any charge against him. Before the hanging, the lynchers were set upon by "a large number of persons," and the noise suggested "a battle was in progress." The would-be leader fled through the brush and had not since been seen near Searcy, and the hanging did not take place.
No report of arrests, injuries or any legal proceedings appears in the coverage, and who attacked the lynchers is not stated.

The Memphis Daily Appeal printed the Searcy Record's paragraph on December 28, 1881, in its "Arkansas Abstracts" column, among items on railroad building, a church appointment and the temperance vote. The Record wrote in a comic register, calling the instigator a "would-be instructor in mob law" whose flight "resembled the path of a hurricane." It quoted the slur in his proposal and closed by saying it was "scarcely necessary" to add that the hanging did not take place. The same column reported, in a separate paragraph, that a Black man named Jim Pettus had been jailed for robbing and beating an old man named Waters near Searcy, but it drew no connection between the two items.
No other report of the episode was found in the white press, and the Black-press collection does not reach back to 1881.
